newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian MinFins stuck as freeze issue unclear.
newsitem.headline: Russian MinFins stuck as freeze issue unclear.

text.p: Trading has largely dried up on the MinFin bond market, dealers said on Monday, as a banking source said an order to freeze $57 million of MinFin bonds had been issued, and a newspaper reported prosecutors investigating a murder case had frozen $54 million of bonds.
Only a few deals were being conducted through brokers on Wednesday because of the uncertainty, dealers said.
Trading has been hit since Monday when rumours began circulating that some banks had been advised that some of their MinFins, totalling more than $50 million face value, had been frozen.
There has been no official comment on the rumours.

Officials in the Finance Ministry, the issuer of the dollar-denominated bonds, declined to comment on Wednesday, saying they had no information on the matter. No comment from Vneshtorgbank, the main MinFin depositary, was available.

A banking source who works closely on MinFin market developments told Reuters on Wednesday that the prosecutor's office in Moscow's Tagansky district had issued an order to freeze almost $57 million of MinFins by face value.
The source would not say when the order was issued but said the bonds are widely distributed among different banks.
The Kommersant-Daily newspaper said on Wednesday the Tagansky prosecutor's office was investigating the murder of two businessmen and had frozen $54 million of MinFins as part of this investigation.

A Russian police officer working on a frozen MinFin case told Reuters on Monday that a larger volume of Russian MinFin bonds may have been frozen this May in addition to the $24 million previously reported.
Dealers said operators were reducing the counterparty risk arising from the possibility of frozen MinFins by restricting trade to brokers.
"Nobody is interested in maintaining the liquidity of the market when good news is unlikely," one dealer said.
Earlier this year the authorities froze $24.22 million of the dollar-denominated bonds, which had gone missing. Many of them were stolen in Chechnya.
The issue has still not been resolved.
In August banking sources said police were preparing to freeze up to another $7 million of MinFin bonds belonging to a small Russian bank and to some foreign trade organisations.
It is not clear whether this order has been issued.
